title: Virtual list, addenda — index as key, forced sync layout, the RAIL budget
body:
> **The main write-up is here: [The virtualized list — Baidu bullet 1](https://apollo-five-omega.vercel.app/library?section=baidu&item=virtual-list)** > > That one covers the full mechanism and how to answer for it: why 500 DOM nodes drop frames, the core idea, the spacer that keeps the scrollbar honest, `transform` vs `top`, IntersectionObserver and the sentinel, a complete `useVirtualList`, variable heights, the quantified 30→60 FPS attribution — plus the build-vs-buy reasoning, the two hard parts, expected follow-ups and a pre-interview checklist. > > **This page is the addenda**, holding only the six points the main write-up does not expand. --- #### ① Why the index is fine as a key here The usual advice is "don't use the index as a key", but the point behind that rule is "a key must uniquely and stably identify one row" — there is nothing inherently wrong with an index. What the rule guards against is a list that reorders, or has items inserted or removed in the middle, while the item contents stay the same. There, the index and the actual row drift apart, React reuses the wrong component instance, and you get misplaced state and jumping animations. In a virtual list, `list` only appends — nothing is inserted in the middle and nothing reorders — so row `items[15]` is index 15 forever, whatever the user scrolls or pages. And a virtual list depends on keys entering and leaving to drive mounting and unmounting: indices that scroll out disappear, indices that scroll in appear. Using the index here is correct, and arguably closer to how the thing actually works. #### ② Why getBoundingClientRect needs care Normally the browser batches DOM and CSS changes and does one layout pass before the frame is drawn. But APIs that read geometry — `getBoundingClientRect()`, `offsetTop`, `scrollHeight` — have to return an accurate, current position and size. If there are pending DOM or style changes, the browser has to apply them and run layout synchronously before it can answer. That is a **forced synchronous layout**, and it is far more expensive than ordinary JavaScript. The classic trap is alternating writes and reads: ```js // bad: every iteration forces a synchronous layout for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) { items[i].style.width = someWidth + 'px'; // write: marks it dirty console.log(items[i].getBoundingClientRect()); // read: forces layout right now } // good: read in one pass, write in another const rects = items.map(item => item.getBoundingClientRect()); items.forEach((item) => { item.style.width = someWidth + 'px'; }); ``` This is also why a virtual list prefers `IntersectionObserver` to checking visibility with `getBoundingClientRect` inside a scroll handler — the latter forces a synchronous layout as soon as it is interleaved with DOM writes, and it costs main-thread time every frame regardless; `IntersectionObserver` does its visibility work off the main thread entirely. #### ③ RAIL and the 60 FPS budget, one level deeper - 60 FPS = 1000ms / 60 ≈ 16.67ms per frame - JavaScript really only gets about 10ms of that; the rest belongs to style, layout, paint, composite, and the browser's own scheduling. Go over budget and you drop a frame — and it takes several dropped frames in a row before the user calls it janky. - **RAIL**: **R**esponse (respond to input within 100ms), **A**nimation (16ms per frame), **I**dle (leave the main thread free for the browser), **L**oad (interactive within 5s on first load, measured on a mid-range phone over slow 3G; 2s for subsequent loads — the 1s figure is from the 2015 original). #### ④ Proving that off-screen nodes really are destroyed There is no teardown function. Destruction falls out of React's `key` diff: every scroll recomputes which indices should show, and any `key` not in `visibleItems` simply is not created on the next render. To see it with your own eyes, add a cleanup in the item component: ```js function FeedCard({ item }) { useEffect(() => { console.log(`mount: item ${item.id}`); return () => console.log(`unmount: item ${item.id}`); // prints when it scrolls out }, []); return
{/* ... */}
; } ``` While scrolling, the console prints "mount: item 15" followed by "unmount: item 2" over and over. That is the most direct code-level evidence that nodes leaving the screen are destroyed. #### ⑤ Going deeper - **Uneven item heights**: see the variable-height section of the [main write-up](https://apollo-five-omega.vercel.app/library?section=baidu&item=virtual-list) (`sizeMap` plus measure-and-backfill). - **Keyboard navigation and focus**: when a recycled item's DOM disappears, focus goes with it. Remember the focused index and restore it on remount, or use `content-visibility: hidden` to hide offscreen content without actually removing the DOM (`contain: layout` is only a layout-isolation hint; it hides nothing). - **Lazy-loading images**: a virtual list mounts only what is visible, which is lazy loading already. Combine it with native `loading="lazy"`, or wrap each image in its own `IntersectionObserver`. - **Dynamic content** (expanding comments changes the height): observe each item with `ResizeObserver`, update `sizeMap` when the height changes, and recompute the offsets. - **Does a virtual list hurt SEO?** Yes. Only the visible items are in the DOM, so a crawler never sees the rest. Either skip virtualisation for SEO-sensitive pages, or fall back to SSR — emit the full content in the HTML and virtualise once the client takes over. - **Why not `content-visibility: auto`?** It is a newer CSS feature that lets the browser skip layout and paint for invisible items — a lighter alternative that suits small and medium lists. Tens of thousands of rows still need real virtualisation. - **White flashes on fast scrolling**: increase the overscan buffer; or degrade to a static placeholder at high scroll speeds; or pre-render a skeleton. - **Infinite scroll vs pagination**: infinite scroll feels smooth but makes it hard to return to a position; pagination is clear and the URL can be shared and revisited. A middle path is updating the URL hash as you scroll, so the back button works. #### ⑥ A reflection: that number was corrected once The resume line originally read **"reducing DOM nodes from 500+ to ~20"**; it now reads **"live DOM nodes stay near 100 at any scroll depth"**. Why that changed is worth remembering. **"~20" counts items, not DOM nodes.** Nine cards at roughly ten elements each is about **a hundred** live nodes, not twenty. On top of that a virtual list normally carries **overscan** — a few extra rows above and below — to avoid blank space during fast scrolling, because rendering exactly the viewport and nothing else tends to flicker. With overscan the real range is around 100–150. **The wording matters more than the number.** "From 500+ down to ~20" sounds like a one-off measurement, but what a virtual list actually changes is the **growth relationship**: node count stops growing as the user scrolls and data accumulates, and is instead pinned to a constant range. Hence the current phrasing — "stay near 100 **at any scroll depth**" — which is the property that carries the value. **The lesson**: know how a number was measured before writing it down. Record the scroll in Chrome DevTools' Performance panel, or just count with `document.querySelectorAll('*').length`. **A wrong number is worse than no number** — one follow-up of "how do twenty nodes render nine cards?" and you are caught. --- --- > This post originally carried three more topics, now split out: > - [Debounce in depth — leading / trailing / cancel](/blog?post=52) - [The toolchain for diagnosing production problems](/blog?post=53) - [Reviewing a full-stack project's choices — tRPC / Zod / React Hook Form](/blog?post=54)
